message.reasoning:
Let me work through this brief carefully.

The task: Write a 400-550 word case-study essay for "Actual Intelligence" by Nicholas Major, about J.P. Morgan's lockbox robots. Drafted by GLM 5.3 Flash (that's me, the standing newsletter drafter). Output prose only, title under 60 characters, Markdown. No invented Nick experience, client work, or private thoughts.

Key editorial proposal: physical document handling and connected processing stages explain the value, with each improvement built on earlier operational work.

Explain what the company did well and why; stop without advice, diagnostic questions, moral, or summary.

Safe facts:
- 130 million checks in 2025 (J.P. Morgan Payments processed)
- 2025: mail automation robot at ONE lockbox site, developed with Ripcord
- Lockbox service explanation
- Robots: open envelopes, remove/unfold contents, separate pages, remove staples, track contents, scan documents
- Robots handle 4,000+ envelope/document permutations
- OMIT the 480 million number (network workload, confusing)
- 2020: rebuilt underlying processing platform, AI for extraction, quality validation, review. Later added LLMs for complex review.
- 13 billion keystrokes annually now largely automated. Attribute to layered platform, not robot or LLM alone. No savings estimate or job replacement claim.
- OMIT 99.999% accuracy (undisclosed measurement)
- Operators have visibility into throughput, exceptions, turnaround time, AI assistant for process info
- Every model tested before deployment; no independent audit claimed

Title options:
1. J.P. Morgan's AI had to remove the staples (43 chars)
2. The paperwork before the payment (32 chars)
3. J.P. Morgan put AI in the mailroom (34 chars)

Which is strongest? Option 1 is the most concrete and specific. "J.P. Morgan's AI had to remove the staples" — it captures the physical reality of the problem, which is the editorial proposal. It's a bit odd because the AI isn't what removes the staples; the robot does. But it's punchy and concrete. Option 3 is plainer but less interesting. Option 2 is decent but vaguer. The brief says choose the strongest automatically. I think option 1 is strongest because it's the most specific and memorable, and it points at the physical-document-handling thesis. It's 43 characters, under 60. Let me go with option 1.

Actually, let me reconsider. "J.P. Morgan's AI had to remove the staples" — the robot removes staples, powered by computer vision and AI models. The title slightly conflates AI and robot. But it's fine as shorthand; the essay can clarify. It's the strongest hook. Go with it.

Voice requirements:
- First person (Nick), one clear position
- Plain language, contractions, sentences opening with but/so/and
- Vary rhythm, punchy one-liners after longer sentences
- One dry aside per piece
- No em dashes
- No "not X but Y"
- No rule of three (careful: the robot task list is naturally a list — open envelopes, remove staples, scan. I need to be careful with listing tasks. The safe facts list many tasks: open envelopes, remove/unfold contents, separate pages, remove staples, track contents, scan. That's six tasks. If I list them, I should list them naturally, not force a triplet. Maybe pick a few or list them all as a natural enumeration. A natural list of what the robot physically does is fine as long as it doesn't read as "adjective, adjective, adjective" triplet. I'll list them as verbs, which is factual.)
- No banned vocabulary
- Sentence-case subheads, one or two max
- Link inline to primary page where it supports exact facts
- Label outcomes bank-reported
- No caveat catalogue
- No advice/diagnostic/moral/summary at the end
- No "the useful part" / "the interesting part"
- No preamble sentences at paragraph level (the mechanical test: delete first sentence of each paragraph, if same or stronger, cut it)
- End on last fact or direct observation about the example
- Bookending: end rhymes with beginning (from Nick's edits). The title is about staples; the ending could call back to staples or the physical work. That would be a nice touch.
- No em dashes anywhere. Also per unslop: avoid parentheses as dash substitutes? The unslop skill says avoid parentheses as dash substitutes too ("reaching for parentheses instead just trades one tell for another"). Hmm, but writing-voice says parentheses are an acceptable replacement for em dashes. The unslop skill says "Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes)." There's a conflict. The core writing-voice rule says parentheses are fine. The unslop skill is about avoiding the *tell*. I'll minimize parentheses use anyway; maybe zero parentheses to be safe. Actually a well-placed parenthetical is natural human writing. But to be safe, I'll avoid or use sparingly. Let me try to write without parentheses.

Structure plan (400-550 words):

Lede: plain lede suggestion given: "J.P. Morgan's payment automation includes a robot that opens envelopes and removes staples." I can use that or a variant. The brief says "Plain lede suggestion" — I can use it. Good, start on the point.

Paragraph 1: The lede. Robot opens envelopes, removes staples. Developed with Ripcord, deployed at one lockbox site in 2025. Link to source. Maybe the dry aside here: something about staples being the hard part. Actually the dry aside could be: "Staple removal is not a glamorous problem, but it's the kind of thing that decides whether automation works." Hmm, that's a bit of a "not X but Y" shape. Careful. Maybe: "It turns out the staples matter." Or weave the position: the interesting thing about this story isn't the AI models, it's the envelopes. Wait, "isn't X, it's Y" is banned. State directly: "The models get the headlines. The envelopes are the story." Hmm, that's a contrast construction but not the banned "not X, it's Y" family exactly... Actually "The models get the headlines. The envelopes are the story." is a contrast but stated as two positive statements. The ban is on "It's not X, it's Y" and family including "Not X. Y." Hmm, "The models get the headlines. The envelopes are the story." — is that "Not X. Y."? It's not literally negating X. It's two statements. I think it's okay but it flirts with the stock contrast construction which the brief also bans ("no stock contrast constructions"). Let me avoid it. State the thesis directly: something like "Most coverage of this would lead with the AI. The physical work is the reason it works." That's still contrast-y. Let me just state the thesis: "The hard part of automating paper is the paper." That's a clean thesis sentence. Or: "Automating the reading was the easy part. The paper is the hard part." Hmm, "easy part / hard part" is a contrast construction. Brief says no stock contrast constructions. Let me be careful.

Thesis, stated plainly: "The value here comes from handling physical documents and connecting each processing stage, not from any single model." — that uses "not from" which is a negation but not the "It's not X, it's Y" template... actually it kind of is: "comes from X, not from Y" is the same family inverted. Hmm. The ban is on "It's not X, it's Y" and family. "The value comes from A and B" — just state A and B. "The value here comes from two places: the physical handling of documents, and the fact that each stage connects to the last." That works without negation.

Actually, the editorial proposal: "physical document handling and connected processing stages explain the value, with each improvement built on earlier operational work." So the essay's one position: what made this work is that J.P. Morgan treated the physical handling as an engineering problem and built each stage on prior operational work. I should state that as Nick's view.

Let me think about what Nick's position would be, grounded in the facts, without inventing his experience. He can have an opinion about the case: e.g., "I like this example because nothing in it is exotic." Or "This is a good example of the in-depth research required to identify where AI can actually make a difference" — that's the register the brief explicitly endorses as the intended closing register (from the voice file: "A direct observation such as 'This is a good example of the in-depth research required to identify where AI can actually make a difference' is the intended register."). Interesting — so the close can be a direct observation like that, about the example. But careful: the brief says stop without advice, diagnostic questions, moral, or summary. A direct observation about the example is fine.

Draft outline:

Title: J.P. Morgan's AI had to remove the staples

Para 1 (lede): J.P. Morgan's payment automation now includes a robot that opens envelopes and removes staples. In 2025 the bank put a mail automation robot at one of its lockbox sites, built with Ripcord. Link. Facts: lockbox explanation can come here or next para.

Para 2: What lockbox is. Companies send payments to a bank-managed address; the bank deposits checks and digitizes paperwork for reconciliation. Over 130 million checks in 2025. This is old, physical, unglamorous work.

Para 3: What the robot does. Opens envelopes, unfolds contents, separates pages, removes staples, tracks contents, scans. Handles 4,000+ envelope and document permutations, per the bank. Why this matters: variability that's trivial for humans is hard to encode. This is the physical handling half of the thesis. Maybe the dry aside here: "Nobody writes conference talks about staple removal." Something dry. Or "It's the least glamorous automation you'll read about this year." Hmm, "you'll read about" is fine. One dry aside per piece. Let me pick one spot.

Para 4: Subhead maybe here: "Built on 2020" or
